newsitem.title: USA: Cohen to press Congress for base closings.
newsitem.headline: Cohen to press Congress for base closings.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Cohen will ask Congress to close more domestic military bases and approve higher spending on national missile defence in a key strategy review this month, the Pentagon said on Tuesday.

"He will seek additional base closures," Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters following warnings from Cohen that more base closures were needed to catch up with U.S. troop cuts made since the end of the Cold War.
Bacon said the Quadrennial Defence Review (QDR) would also seek between $1 billion and $2 billion in additional funding to develop a possible national defence against missile attack.

The QDR, scheduled to go to Congress on May 15, is aimed at maintaining a superpower military force and forward deployment. It will include cost-cutting in areas such as basing and civilian bureaucracy to pay for new fighter jets and other arms.
The Defence Department has already shut or is closing dozens of big domestic bases and hundreds of smaller facilities in four rounds of domestic closings that are scheduled to be completed in 2001.

Bacon declined to give details of the new call, but other defence officials said privately that Cohen intended to press lawmakers to approve an additional two rounds of politically-explosive domestic closings, one beginning in 1999 and the other in 2001.
Such moves are economically devastating for many communities, which depend on military payrolls and purchasing power.

But Cohen noted in recent speeches that the U.S. armed forces has slashed troop strength by one-third to 1.4 million since the Soviet Union collapsed, but only 18 percent of basing structure has been cut at home and abroad.
Hundreds of big and small U.S. military facilities have also been closed overseas in recent years. The secretary can order the closure of overseas bases without approval from Congress.

Congress earlier passed laws that allowed for the four rounds of domestic closings overseen by base closing and realignment commissions (BRAC). The independent commissions would draw up closing lists that would have to be either approved or rejected as a whole by Congress.
The issue is a politically explosive one in Congress and defence officials have conceded it will be difficult to get lawmakers to authorise a new BRAC round or rounds.

On the missile defence issue, the Washington Times reported on Tuesday that the Pentagon was behind budget and schedule on a plan to develop technologies and weapons for a possible national missile defence by 1999.

Bacon said the QDR would recommend additional spending of between $1 billion and $2 billion to prepare technology for a potential national missile defence by 1999 in case the Pentagon decided then that such a system should be deployed by the year 2003.

The Clinton administration has rejected pressure from Congressional Republicans to revive former President Ronald Reagan's dream of a so-called "Star Wars" anti-missile umbrella over the United States, opting instead for a less-ambitious programme to protect troops and bases.
But the Pentagon has agreed to work on technologies for a national missile defence and to have them ready for a decision by 1999 to deploy later if the need arises.
